Lecture 19

Residues and real integrals

Lecture objectives

We prove the residue theorem on star-shaped sets, compute the winding numbers of circles and half-discs, and define the residue at infinity. We evaluate trigonometric integrals over a period and rational integrals over the real line, and we prove the arc estimates they need, including Jordan’s estimate for the factor eikz.\ee^{\iu kz}eikz.

Lecture 18 expanded a function about an isolated singular point in a Laurent series and called the coefficient of (z−z0)−1(z-z_0)^{-1}(z−z0​)−1 the residue. In this lecture we prove that the integral of a function around a closed path is 2πi2\pi\iu2πi times the sum of its residues, each counted with the winding number of the path. We then evaluate real integrals with it: integrals over a period of trigonometric expressions, and integrals of rational functions over the real line, with and without an oscillating factor eikx.\ee^{\iu kx}eikx. For the line integrals the segment [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] is closed by a semicircle whose integral must tend to zero.

19.1 The residue theorem

We recall the terms of Lecture 18. Let fff be analytic on a punctured disc 0<∣z−z0∣<r.0<\abs{z-z_0}<r0<∣z−z0​∣<r. By Laurent’s theorem it is the sum of its Laurent series ∑n∈Zan(z−z0)n\sum_{n\in\Z}a_n(z-z_0)^n∑n∈Z​an​(z−z0​)n there. The part ∑n≥1a−n(z−z0)−n\sum_{n\ge1}a_{-n}(z-z_0)^{-n}∑n≥1​a−n​(z−z0​)−n is the principal part of fff at z0,z_0z0​, and the residue is Res⁡z=z0f=a−1=12πi∮Cρ(z0)f(z) ⁣dz(0<ρ<r).\Res_{z=z_0}f=a_{-1}=\frac1{2\pi\iu}\oint_{C_\rho(z_0)}f(z)\dd z\qquad(0<\rho<r).Resz=z0​​f=a−1​=2πi1​∮Cρ​(z0​)​f(z)dz(0<ρ<r).

Theorem 19.1 (Residue theorem). Let UUU be an open set that is star-shaped, let z1,…,zm∈Uz_1,\ldots,z_m\in Uz1​,…,zm​∈U be distinct points, and let fff be analytic on U∖{z1,…,zm}.U\setminus\{z_1,\ldots,z_m\}U∖{z1​,…,zm​}. Then for every closed path CCC in UUU that passes through none of the points zk,z_kzk​, ∮Cf(z) ⁣dz=2πi∑k=1mn(C,zk)Res⁡z=zkf.\oint_Cf(z)\dd z=2\pi\iu\sum_{k=1}^mn(C,z_k)\Res_{z=z_k}f .∮C​f(z)dz=2πik=1∑m​n(C,zk​)Resz=zk​​f.(19.1)

Proof. We subtract the principal parts from fff and apply Cauchy’s theorem to the remainder.

Step 1: the principal parts. Choose r>0r>0r>0 so small that the discs Br(zk)B_r(z_k)Br​(zk​) lie in UUU and are disjoint. On 0<∣z−zk∣<r0<\abs{z-z_k}<r0<∣z−zk​∣<r Laurent’s theorem writes f=φk+Pk,f=\varphi_k+\mathcal P_kf=φk​+Pk​, where the regular part φk\varphi_kφk​ is analytic on Br(zk)B_r(z_k)Br​(zk​) and Pk(z)=∑n=1∞a−n(k)(z−zk)−n\mathcal P_k(z)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty a^{(k)}_{-n}(z-z_k)^{-n}Pk​(z)=n=1∑∞​a−n(k)​(z−zk​)−n is the principal part. The superscript (k)(k)(k) labels the point zk.z_kzk​. By Laurent’s theorem with inner radius 0,00, this series converges for every z≠zk.z\ne z_kz=zk​. It is a power series in w=1/(z−zk)w=1/(z-z_k)w=1/(z−zk​) that converges for every w,ww, so its radius of convergence is infinite. By the propositions of Lecture 18 on the convergence of a power series and on power series being analytic, it converges uniformly on each set ∣w∣≤1/ρ\abs w\le1/\rho∣w∣≤1/ρ with ρ>0,\rho>0ρ>0, that is, on ∣z−zk∣≥ρ,\abs{z-z_k}\ge\rho∣z−zk​∣≥ρ, and its sum is analytic in w.ww. By the chain rule of Lecture 15, Pk\mathcal P_kPk​ is analytic on C∖{zk}.\C\setminus\{z_k\}C∖{zk​}.

Step 2: the remainder. Put g=f−P1−⋯−Pmg=f-\mathcal P_1-\cdots-\mathcal P_mg=f−P1​−⋯−Pm​ on U∖{z1,…,zm}.U\setminus\{z_1,\ldots,z_m\}U∖{z1​,…,zm​}. On 0<∣z−zk∣<r,0<\abs{z-z_k}<r0<∣z−zk​∣<r, g=φk−∑j≠kPj,g=\varphi_k-\sum_{j\ne k}\mathcal P_j ,g=φk​−j=k∑​Pj​, and the right side is analytic on the whole disc Br(zk),B_r(z_k)Br​(zk​), since zj∉Br(zk)z_j\notin B_r(z_k)zj​∈/Br​(zk​) for j≠k.j\ne kj=k. The set UUU must be star-shaped and must contain the points zk,z_kzk​, where fff need not be defined. On the annulus U={1<∣z∣<3},U=\{1<\abs z<3\}U={1<∣z∣<3}, which is not star-shaped, the function 1/z1/z1/z has no singular point in U,UU, yet ∮C2(0) ⁣dz/z=2πi.\oint_{C_2(0)}\dd z/z=2\pi\iu∮C2​(0)​dz/z=2πi. Its residue lies at 0∉U.0\notin U0∈/U.

Each singular point counts with the winding number of the path around it. For a circle Lecture 17 computed these numbers: Cr(z0)C_r(z_0)Cr​(z0​) winds once around every point of Br(z0)B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​) and zero times around every point outside B‾r(z0).\overline B_r(z_0)Br​(z0​). A disc and the plane are star-shaped, so the theorem gives the following form.

19.2 The point at infinity

A large circle encloses all singular points of a function with finitely many of them. Its integral is then decided by the behaviour of the function for large ∣z∣.\abs z∣z∣. We add a point ∞\infty∞ to the plane and obtain the extended plane C∪{∞}.\C\cup\{\infty\}C∪{∞}. The substitution z=1/wz=1/wz=1/w maps the set ∣z∣>R0\abs z>R_0∣z∣>R0​ onto the punctured disc 0<∣w∣<1/R0,0<\abs w<1/R_00<∣w∣<1/R0​, and the point ∞\infty∞ corresponds to w=0.w=0w=0.

Let fff be analytic on ∣z∣>R0.\abs z>R_0∣z∣>R0​. Then g(w)=f(1/w)g(w)=f(1/w)g(w)=f(1/w) is analytic on 0<∣w∣<1/R0,0<\abs w<1/R_00<∣w∣<1/R0​, so w=0w=0w=0 is an isolated singular point of g.gg. We say that fff has a removable singularity, a pole of order mmm or an essential singularity at ∞\infty∞ when ggg has one at 0.00. For example, a polynomial of degree m≥1m\ge1m≥1 has a pole of order mmm at ∞,\infty∞, the function ez\ee^zez has an essential singularity there, and 1/z1/z1/z has a removable one, since g(w)=w.g(w)=wg(w)=w.

Definition 19.4 (Residue at infinity). Let fff be analytic on ∣z∣>R0,\abs z>R_0∣z∣>R0​, with the Laurent series ∑n∈Zanzn\sum_{n\in\Z}a_nz^n∑n∈Z​an​zn there. The residue of fff at infinity is Res⁡z=∞f=−a−1=−12πi∮Cρ(0)f(z) ⁣dz(ρ>R0).\Res_{z=\infty}f=-a_{-1}=-\frac1{2\pi\iu}\oint_{C_\rho(0)}f(z)\dd z\qquad(\rho>R_0).Resz=∞​f=−a−1​=−2πi1​∮Cρ​(0)​f(z)dz(ρ>R0​).(19.5)

The two expressions agree by Laurent’s theorem with r1=R0r_1=R_0r1​=R0​ and r2=∞,r_2=\inftyr2​=∞, and they do not depend on ρ.\rhoρ. The minus sign comes from the orientation. The circle Cρ(0)C_\rho(0)Cρ​(0) traversed clockwise keeps the set ∣z∣>ρ,\abs z>\rho∣z∣>ρ, which surrounds ∞,\infty∞, on its left. So the clockwise direction is the positive orientation around ∞,\infty∞, and (19.5) is the integral in that direction divided by 2πi,2\pi\iu2πi, as for a finite point. Ablowitz and Fokas (§4.1) use the opposite sign.

19.4 Rational integrals over the real line

To evaluate ∫−∞∞P(x)/Q(x) ⁣dx\int_{-\infty}^\infty P(x)/Q(x)\dd x∫−∞∞​P(x)/Q(x)dx we close the segment [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] with the arc ARA_RAR​ and let R→∞.R\to\inftyR→∞. Two facts must be shown. The integral over ARA_RAR​ must tend to zero, and the integrals over [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] must tend to the improper integral. The second fact needs care. An improper integral over the line requires both limits, at +∞+\infty+∞ and at −∞,-\infty−∞, separately (GM 27), but the contour gives only the symmetric integral ∫−RR.\int_{-R}^R∫−RR​. For x/(x2+1)x/(x^2+1)x/(x2+1) the symmetric integral is 000 for every R,RR, because the integrand is odd, while ∫0Rx ⁣dx/(x2+1)=12ln⁡(R2+1)\int_0^R x\dd x/(x^2+1)=\frac12\ln(R^2+1)∫0R​xdx/(x2+1)=21​ln(R2+1) tends to infinity. Proposition 19.15 (Rational integrals with an oscillating factor). Example 19.17 (An integral that needs Jordan’s estimate). Let a>0a>0a>0 and k>0.k>0k>0. The arc estimate shows why Jordan’s estimate is needed. On ARA_RAR​ with R>aR>aR>a we have ∣h∣≤R/(R2−a2).\abs h\le R/(R^2-a^2)∣h∣≤R/(R2−a2). As k→0+k\to0^+k→0+ the value tends to π,\piπ, but at k=0k=0k=0 the integrand is 0,00, and for k<0k<0k<0 the integral is −πeka,-\pi\ee^{ka}−πeka, because sin⁡\sinsin is odd. The integral is discontinuous at k=0,k=0k=0, so a limit k→0k\to0k→0 cannot be taken under the integral sign here. ◃

Jordan’s estimate is a sufficient bound for one situation: a semicircular arc and an integrand eikzg(z)\ee^{\iu kz}g(z)eikzg(z) with max⁡AR∣g∣→0.\max_{A_R}\abs g\to0maxAR​​∣g∣→0. It does not permit closing a contour in general. The Bromwich inversion of Lecture 27 integrates estF(s)\ee^{st}F(s)estF(s) along a vertical line in the plane of the Laplace variable s.ss. Closing that path needs its own check of the growth of FFF on the added arcs, and Lecture 27 states and checks it for each class of transforms FFF it uses.

Summary

The residue theorem turns a closed contour integral into a sum of residues weighted by winding numbers. Real integrals over a period become integrals around the unit circle. Real integrals over the line are closed by a semicircle in the half-plane where the integrand decays. The arc integral tends to zero by the length estimate or, with a factor eikz,\ee^{\iu kz}eikz, by Jordan’s estimate.

  • Residue theorem: ∮Cf ⁣dz=2πi∑kn(C,zk)Res⁡z=zkf\oint_Cf\dd z=2\pi\iu\sum_kn(C,z_k)\Res_{z=z_k}f∮C​fdz=2πi∑k​n(C,zk​)Resz=zk​​f for fff analytic on a star-shaped open set UUU except at z1,…,zm∈Uz_1,\ldots,z_m\in Uz1​,…,zm​∈U and a closed path CCC in UUU avoiding them.

  • Winding numbers: Cr(z0)C_r(z_0)Cr​(z0​) and ∂DR\partial D_R∂DR​ wind once around the points of the open disc and the open upper half-disc; the clockwise path −∂DR−-\partial D_R^-−∂DR−​ winds −1-1−1 times around the points of the open lower half-disc.

  • Infinity: Res⁡z=∞f=−a−1=−Res⁡w=0f(1/w)/w2;\Res_{z=\infty}f=-a_{-1}=-\Res_{w=0}f(1/w)/w^2Resz=∞​f=−a−1​=−Resw=0​f(1/w)/w2; for fff analytic on C\CC except at finitely many points, the residue at infinity and all finite residues add up to zero; Res⁡z=∞f=0\Res_{z=\infty}f=0Resz=∞​f=0 when ∣f∣≤K/∣z∣2\abs f\le K/\abs z^2∣f∣≤K/∣z∣2 for large ∣z∣.\abs z∣z∣.

  • Real integrals: over a period with z=eiθ;z=\ee^{\iu\theta}z=eiθ; ∫RP/Q ⁣dx=2πi∑Im⁡zj>0Res⁡P/Q\int_{\R}P/Q\dd x=2\pi\iu\sum_{\Im z_j>0}\Res P/Q∫R​P/Qdx=2πi∑Imzj​>0​ResP/Q when deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+2\deg Q\ge\deg P+2degQ≥degP+2 and QQQ has no real zero; with eikx,\ee^{\iu kx}eikx, k>0,k>0k>0, the same formula holds for deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+1\deg Q\ge\deg P+1degQ≥degP+1 by Jordan’s estimate, and k<0k<0k<0 closes below with a minus sign.

Lecture 20 lets the path pass singular points on the real axis on small semicircles, compares ordinary and principal-value integrals, and integrates along the two banks of a branch cut.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. A closed contour is made by taking the unit circle twice clockwise. The function is analytic on a neighbourhood of the closed unit disc apart from simple poles at 000 and 1/21/21/2. Which weights for the two residues enter the residue theorem?

Hint. Count the turns of the contour as seen from each pole, with orientation.

Neither pole lies on the contour, and both lie in the disc. Each clockwise circuit has winding number −1-1−1 about each pole. The residue theorem weights each residue by its total winding number, so both weights are −2-2−2. Positive weights would count counterclockwise turns. The weight −1-1−1 counts just one circuit.

2. Using the unit circle, evaluate ∫02π(3−2cos⁡θ)−1 ⁣dθ\int_0^{2\pi}(3-2\cos\theta)^{-1}\dd\theta∫02π​(3−2cosθ)−1dθ. Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Use z=eiθz=\ee^{\iu\theta}z=eiθ and check which root of the resulting quadratic lies inside the circle.

Substituting 2cos⁡θ=z+z−12\cos\theta=z+z^{-1}2cosθ=z+z−1 and  ⁣dθ= ⁣dz/(iz)\dd\theta=\dd z/(\iu z)dθ=dz/(iz) gives the integral of  ⁣dz/[i(3z−z2−1)]\dd z/[\iu(3z-z^2-1)]dz/[i(3z−z2−1)] around the unit circle. The roots are (3±5)/2(3\pm\sqrt5)/2(3±5​)/2. Only a=(3−5)/2a=(3-\sqrt5)/2a=(3−5​)/2 is inside. The simple residue is 1/[i(3−2a)]=1/(i5)1/[\iu(3-2a)]=1/(\iu\sqrt5)1/[i(3−2a)]=1/(i5​). Multiplication by 2πi2\pi\iu2πi gives 2π/52\pi/\sqrt52π/5​.

3. For the real-line integral of eikxP(x)/Q(x)\ee^{\iu kx}P(x)/Q(x)eikxP(x)/Q(x) with k<0k<0k<0, no real poles and deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+2\deg Q\ge\deg P+2degQ≥degP+2, how should you close the path if the real segment is traversed from left to right?

Hint. For z=x+iyz=x+\iu yz=x+iy, check the sign of −ky-ky−ky and trace the arc back to the starting point.

The modulus of the exponential is e−ky\ee^{-ky}e−ky. For y≤0y\le0y≤0 it is at most one, so the rational bound O(R−2)O(R^{-2})O(R−2) times the arc length πR\pi RπR tends to zero. Closing from right to left below the axis gives clockwise orientation. In the upper half-plane the exponential grows, so the quadratic rational bound gives no vanishing estimate there.

4. What is the residue at infinity of f(z)=1/(z−1)+2/(z+1)f(z)=1/(z-1)+2/(z+1)f(z)=1/(z−1)+2/(z+1)?

Hint. Add the residues at all finite poles and relate their sum to the residue at infinity.

At z=1z=1z=1 the residue is 111, and at z=−1z=-1z=−1 it is 222. Their sum plus the residue at infinity is zero, so the latter is −3-3−3. The value 333 keeps the finite sum’s sign. The value 000 mistakes decay of fff for vanishing of the residue, and −1-1−1 uses only the pole at z=1z=1z=1.
